This paper uses weave-pattern analysis to correct the topology after 3D reconstruction, ensuring the simulated cloth behaves like the real thing.
ReWeaver — Topology-Accurate Garment Rec.how: The problem: Standard 3D reconstruction from video (e.g., neural radiance fields) infers the surface by matching pixels across frames, but this process is indifferent to topology — it can produce meshes where nearby vertices are far in the connectivity, or where long-range edges cross. When such a mesh is simulated, the crossing edges create unphysical constraints, and the cloth tears or sticks to itself. The mechanism: ReWeaver takes a reconstructed mesh and analyzes the local fabric structure in the input video frames: (1) Weave pattern detection uses a small CNN trained on woven fabric to identify the local weave orientation (warp and weft directions) and spacing in each video frame. (2) Projection onto the mesh maps these orientations and spacings to the 3D mesh vertices. (3) Topology repair adjusts the edge connectivity to align with the detected weave structure: if the weave spacing is 2 mm, vertices within 3 mm should be neighbors; if weave direction is 45°, edges should follow that direction. (4) Validation checks that the repaired mesh has no self-intersections and satisfies manifold constraints (every edge bordered by exactly two triangles). The corrected mesh is then simulation-ready: cloth simulations using the corrected mesh preserve folds, drape realistically, and do not tear. Why it works: Weave structure is stable across view angles (even if 3D position is uncertain, the weave pattern is still locally evident in the pixel data), so correcting topology based on detected weave is more reliable than trying to infer it from the 3D shape alone.

RealAppliance — Workable Appliance Asset.narr: Benchmarking robot manipulation requires models of real appliances (blenders, ovens, dishwashers) with correct kinematic structure. Building these by hand is expensive. This paper extracts kinematic structure from RGB video of a person using an appliance — detecting which parts move, the joint type (hinge, slider), and the range of motion. The result is a URDF that enables simulation-based benchmarking: a robot can be trained on the simulated appliance and then deployed on the real one with minimal sim-to-real gap.
RealAppliance — Workable Appliance Asset.how: The problem: An appliance like a dishwasher has one actuated door and several internal parts that move independently or coupled to the door. A vision system must infer not just the door's hinge axis, but also the kinematic tree: which parts move together, which parts are spring-loaded, what are the joint limits. Manual annotation requires disassembly or extensive labeling. The mechanism: The pipeline processes a 30-second video of someone using the appliance: (1) Motion segmentation: optical flow is computed frame-to-frame, and regions with similar flow are clustered. Each cluster represents a moving part. (2) Articulation model fitting: for each moving part, fit a rigid motion model (assuming the part rotates around a single axis). The hinge axis direction and position are recovered by finding the rotation center that best explains the observed motion across all frames. For a dishwasher door opening, the axis is recovered within 2° error. (3) Joint limits: the range of angles observed across all frames gives the joint limits. (4) Spring analysis: if the part returns to the same position when released, a spring is modeled; if it stays, the joint is actuated. (5) URDF assembly: the kinematic tree is encoded as a URDF with revolute and prismatic joints. When a robot simulator loads the URDF, it has the correct joint structure and can generate trajectories that avoid collisions with moving parts. Why it works: Moving parts in video naturally cluster by motion; the motion is rigid (a door does not deform), so fitting rigid rotation to motion recovery is well-posed. The joint axis is determined by the locus of rotation centers across frames — a stable quantity that is reliable to noise.

NeuROK — Generative 4D Neural Object Kin.narr: When a robot pushes on an object, the object deforms. Predicting how much it deforms and where is essential for manipulation, but the deformation depends on unknown material properties (Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio). This paper learns to predict per-point motion fields from a single static 3D observation: given the object's resting shape and one probe application, the model predicts how every point on the object will move under different forces, without explicit material estimation.
NeuROK — Generative 4D Neural Object Kin.how: The problem: Deformable object manipulation requires knowing how the object responds to contact. A purely geometric approach (ignoring material properties) predicts no deformation. Explicit material estimation requires multiple probe measurements, which is slow. The mechanism: NeuROK trains a neural field (an MLP that maps 3D position to 3D motion vector) on a dataset of simulated deformable objects: a sphere of rubber (E = 10 kPa), a stiffer cube (E = 100 kPa), etc. For each object, it generates training data by simulating contact at many points and recording the resulting displacement field. The MLP learns a latent code z for each object that captures its material properties. At test time, given a single 3D observation of a new object: (1) A probe applies 0.5 N at a test point and observes the local deformation (depth camera). (2) An encoder network infers the latent code z from the single observation and the probe response. (3) The neural field, conditioned on z, outputs the motion at every point under any force query (0.5 N, 1.0 N, 2.0 N). Why it works: The latent code implicitly captures material properties; the neural field learns smooth motion fields from simulation, and a single real probe measurement is enough to infer the latent code for a unseen object. The result is a compact model (one code vector per object) that generalizes to unseen force levels.

PhysSkin — Physics-Based Neural Skinning.narr: Character animation typically uses hand-crafted blend-shape deformations: an animator specifies how the character's skin deforms at each joint angle, and the renderer interpolates. This is labor-intensive and breaks when the character is deformed beyond the training poses. This paper embeds physical plausibility constraints into neural skinning: as the character moves, the skin deformation is constrained to be consistent with elastic material properties estimated from video. The result is a skinning model that respects physics and generalizes to unseen poses without hand-tuning.
PhysSkin — Physics-Based Neural Skinning.how: The problem: Neural networks can learn arbitrary deformations from data, but learned deformations often violate physical constraints: skin can stretch infinitely, or compress below zero volume. These artifacts break immersion and make sim-to-real transfer difficult. The mechanism: The pipeline takes video of a character moving (e.g., a person bending their arm) and jointly optimizes two things: (1) Neural skinning weights: an MLP that predicts, for each vertex and joint angle, the blending weight (how much that joint influences that vertex). (2) Material properties: Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio ν. During optimization, for each frame: (a) compute vertex positions using the learned weights and observed joint angles; (b) measure local strain (stretch and compression) by comparing edge lengths to rest state; (c) apply a constitutive model (linear elasticity) to predict stress from strain; (d) check that predicted stress is physically plausible (stress matches material properties); (e) backprop gradient to adjust weights and material properties. Over frames, the optimizer learns skinning weights that, when applied to the character, produce deformations consistent with E ≈ 10 kPa (soft tissue). When deployed on a pose not in the training video, the skinning weights generalize, and the learned material properties ensure the deformation stays physically plausible. Why it works: Physics provides a strong regularizer: instead of fitting to pixels arbitrarily, the network fits to pixels while respecting the constraint that deformation is elastic. This shared inductive bias helps generalization.

UniPixie — Probabilistic 3D Physics via.narr: Inferring material properties from a single image is ill-posed: many different material parameters (density, stiffness, friction) could produce the same visual appearance. Instead of predicting a point estimate, this paper predicts a distribution over plausible material parameters. A normalizing flow learns the posterior distribution of material properties given visual observations, allowing a controller to either pick the maximum-likelihood estimate or sample from the distribution to hedge against uncertainty.
UniPixie — Probabilistic 3D Physics via.how: The problem: A standard neural network maps image → material parameters as a point prediction; if the image is ambiguous, the network must choose one explanation. In reality, multiple material sets are consistent with the observation. The mechanism: UniPixie uses a normalizing flow — a neural network that learns a transformation from a simple distribution (e.g., standard Gaussian) to the posterior distribution of material parameters. Training uses contrastive divergence: (1) Generate a 3D object with ground-truth material properties (E, ν, ρ, μ_friction). (2) Render it from multiple camera angles and apply physics simulation (drop it, let it roll, apply contact forces). (3) Condition the flow on the rendered images: the flow learns to map Gaussian samples to parameter values that, when simulated with those images, produce physically consistent results. (4) During test time, given a real image, the flow samples 100 parameter sets from the posterior and simulates each. The samples cluster around plausible material values: E ∈ [80, 120] kPa (if the object is stiff), or E ∈ [5, 15] kPa (if it deforms easily), depending on observed behavior. A controller can then plan under uncertainty by sampling trajectories for each material hypothesis and picking a reliable action. Why it works: Normalizing flows provide a tractable way to represent complex multimodal distributions; the contrastive learning objective ensures the flow learns parameters that are consistent with observed behavior, not just visually plausible parameters.

Haptic Neural Fields — Tactile Propertie.narr: Scene representations (NeRF, Gaussian splats) model what a camera sees. A robot hand needs to know not just where objects are but how they feel: which surfaces are soft, which are slippery. This paper extends 3D scene representations to include per-point tactile properties (stiffness, friction, damping). A robot can then query the scene representation before touching: “if I push here, how much will it deform?” and adjust its approach accordingly.
Haptic Neural Fields — Tactile Propertie.how: The problem: Vision-only scene representations do not capture material properties; a robot trained only on images cannot predict contact forces or deformation. Including tactile properties requires additional sensing (probing each point) or simulation (expensive). The mechanism: Haptic Neural Fields extend NeRF or Gaussian splat representations with additional per-point parameters: (1) Stiffness field k(x,y,z): an MLP that outputs spring stiffness for each 3D point, trained from tactile sensor data. When a force F is applied at location (x, y, z), the deformation δ = F / k(x, y, z). (2) Friction field μ(x, y, z): a learned coefficient of friction. (3) Damping field c(x, y, z): resistance to motion. Training data comes from real-robot interaction: a finger probes a surface at many locations, measuring stiffness (spring constant from force-displacement), friction (tangential force to slip), and damping (velocity during slow pull). These measurements are registered to the 3D coordinates in the NeRF/Gaussian representation. The MLPs are trained to predict these properties at unseen 3D coordinates. At test time, given a scene represented as a NeRF + Haptic fields, a manipulation planner queries “if I apply 5 N here, deformation = 5 / k(x) = 5 / 50 = 0.1 cm” and can adjust push direction to avoid overstressing fragile regions. Why it works: Tactile properties vary spatially (a surface can be stiff in one place and soft in another); embedding them as learned fields in the same coordinate system as the visual representation couples vision and touch naturally. A robot can "see" the spatial structure and "feel" the material properties in a unified representation.

FUN REC — Functional 3D Scene Reconstruc.narr: Passively observing a scene with a camera reveals geometry but not function: a closed cabinet door looks identical whether the hinge is on the left or right, loose or tight. This paper reconstructs articulation structure (joint type, axis, range, damping) by analyzing video of a human interacting with the scene. Watching someone open and close a cabinet door 5 times reveals where the hinge is, how far it opens, and how much friction it has — all without ever accessing the object's interior or CAD model.
FUN REC — Functional 3D Scene Reconstruc.how: The problem: 3D reconstruction from video infers vertex positions and surface normals, but not which vertices move together or how they are constrained to move. An articulation model requires knowing the joint axis, range of motion, and stiffness — quantities that cannot be inferred from geometry alone. The mechanism: The pipeline processes a video of a human using an object (opening a cabinet door, pushing a drawer): (1) Human pose tracking (ViTPose) estimates hand position and orientation frame-by-frame. (2) Object pose tracking (DOPE) estimates the cabinet's position and orientation in each frame. (3) Contact frame detection: frames where hand and object are in contact are identified using distance thresholding. (4) Part segmentation: regions of the object that move rigidly (the door, the cabinet body) are clustered from optical flow. (5) Articulation fitting: for the door part, fit a revolute joint model by finding the rotation axis that best explains the observed motion across frames. The axis is found by least-squares minimization: for each frame, the door's pose is known; assume it rotates around an axis α, and find α such that the sum of squared errors (observed pose – predicted pose from rotation) is minimized. (6) Range and damping: the observed joint angle trajectory gives the range (min and max angle observed). If the door returns to rest position after being released, a spring-damper model is fit to the return trajectory. Why it works: Human manipulation provides ground truth for how parts move; by observing the contact points and the resulting motion, the system can infer the kinematic constraints that the human follows. The fitted axis is consistent across the entire manipulation sequence, ensuring reliability.

PhysGaia — Physics-Aware Dynamic Scene G.narr: Generative models for 3D scenes often produce visually plausible results that violate physical laws: objects fall through floors, stacked blocks float, or knocked items do not slide. This paper introduces a benchmark for physics-aware scene generation: given a scene description (e.g., “a table with a vase on it”), generate 3D models where objects obey conservation laws under interaction. Evaluating such models is hard; the benchmark includes physics simulators that score whether generated scenes respect gravity, contact, and friction.
PhysGaia — Physics-Aware Dynamic Scene G.how: The problem: Scene generation models are typically trained on images or 3D reconstructions, which do not include physical annotations. The models learn to place objects plausibly in images (e.g., a cup on a table) but not necessarily in physically valid configurations. When the scene is simulated (gravity applied, objects dropped), violations emerge: the cup could be floating just above the table, or clipping into it. The mechanism: PhysGaia provides a dataset and evaluation protocol: (1) Generation task: a diffusion model or other generative model takes a scene description (text or rough sketch) and produces 3D assets + poses for furniture and small objects. (2) Physics validation: the scene is loaded into a physics engine (PyBullet) with gravity enabled. Objects are allowed to settle under gravity for 1 second of simulated time. (3) Metrics: After settling, the system checks for contact violations (overlap between objects), energy violations (objects have moved to lower potential energy than initial state, implying forces were generated from nothing), and trajectory feasibility (if a person is shown pushing an object, the object's trajectory under estimated push forces matches the observed trajectory in the video). (4) Training with physics loss: A generative model trained to maximize these physics metrics learns to place objects in valid configurations: the vase sits firmly on the table (no floating), the stack of blocks is stable (center of mass over support), and pushed objects slide correctly. Why it works: Physics provides an objective loss function; by backpropagating through the physics engine, generative models learn to produce physically valid scenes. The benchmark enables direct comparison of how different models respect conservation laws.

GaussianFluent — Fracture Physics with G.narr: Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a fast 3D rendering method that represents scenes as point clouds with learned colors and covariances. Extending it to support fracture (objects breaking under stress) requires embedding stress fields and fracture criteria into the Gaussian representation. This paper shows how to query the stress at each splat location under simulated contact forces, predict failure points, and render the object after fracture — all without mesh topology or explicit FEM.
GaussianFluent — Fracture Physics with G.how: The problem: Traditional fracture simulation requires a finite element mesh: stress is computed at each element, and if stress exceeds the material's strength, the element breaks. Gaussian Splatting does not have a mesh; it is a point cloud. Simulating fracture with Gaussian splats requires a different approach. The mechanism: The pipeline augments each Gaussian splat with a stress state (σ_xx, σ_yy, σ_zz, σ_xy, σ_yz, σ_zx — the stress tensor at that point). During training on static scenes, the stress is zero. When the scene is subjected to contact forces (a finger pushes on a ceramic mug): (1) Force propagation: contact forces at the splats nearest the finger are initialized. (2) Stress diffusion: stress propagates to neighboring splats through a learned spatial kernel (a neural network that predicts how stress at one location influences stress at nearby locations, mimicking linear elasticity). (3) Fracture detection: von Mises stress σ_VM = √((σ_1 – σ_2)² + (σ_2 – σ_3)² + (σ_3 – σ_1)²)/2) is computed at each splat. If σ_VM > σ_strength (material parameter), the splat is marked as fractured. (4) Rendering after fracture: fractured splats are rendered with a darkened color and reduced opacity, giving the visual appearance of a crack. Why it works: The stress field is learned implicitly through the neural diffusion kernel; the kernel is trained on synthetic data (Gaussian splats representing objects of known material, subjected to known forces with ground-truth FEM-computed stress). At test time, the learned kernel generalizes to new objects and forces without requiring mesh topology or expensive FEM solves.

AssemblyBench — Physics-Aware Assembly o.narr: Assembling two parts requires predicting force and constraint during insertion: if a bolt is misaligned, it will jam; if inserted too fast, threads will strip. Physics-aware scene models must predict these contact forces correctly. This paper introduces a benchmark of assembly tasks (gears meshing, parts stacking, bolt insertion) with ground-truth force measurements. Models are scored on whether their predicted forces match the measured forces during assembly — a stringent test of physical accuracy.
AssemblyBench — Physics-Aware Assembly o.how: The problem: Assembly tasks are common in robotics, but predicting whether an assembly will succeed requires accurate contact force simulation. Many scene models output plausible geometry but incorrect forces (e.g., predicting a bolt will slide freely when it actually jams due to thread engagement). The mechanism: AssemblyBench provides: (1) Assembly scenarios: 20 canonical assembly tasks (gear meshing, bearing insertion, bolt tightening, part stacking, snap-fit closure) represented as URDF files with ground-truth masses, friction coefficients, and joint models. (2) Physical ground truth: for each scenario, a robot arm is teleoperated to perform the assembly while force-torque sensors at the tool flange record the full force-torque vector. The recorded trajectory and forces are stored. (3) Evaluation protocol: a scene model (e.g., a 3D reconstruction + physics property estimator) predicts the masses, friction, and geometry of the two parts. The model then simulates the assembly using MuJoCo or PyBullet. The simulated force-torque trajectory is compared to the ground-truth recorded trajectory (aligned via DTW time warping). Metrics: peak force error, impulse error, and assembly success rate (did the simulation reach the goal state matching the recorded assembly). Why it works: Assembly forces depend on contact geometry, friction, and stiffness — all of which must be inferred correctly. The benchmark reveals whether a model captures these subtleties or merely predicts plausible-looking geometry. Models trained to minimize assembly force error learn to predict material properties and contact parameters more accurately.
